nodes.name: Dimer hex tiling (tiling of a hexagon by $120^\circ-60^\circ$ diamonds)
nodes.statement: The combinatorics of tilings of a hexagon of integer side-length $n$ by $120^\circ-60^\circ$ diamonds of side-length $1$ has a long history, both directly (as a problem of interest in thermodynamic models) and indirectly (through the equivalence to plane partitions \cite{David89}).
nodes.statement_short: The objects counted are tilings of a side-$n$ hexagon by unit $120^\circ-60^\circ$ diamonds, equivalent to plane partitions.
nodes.definiendum: tilings of a hexagon of integer side-length $n$ by $120^\circ-60^\circ$ diamonds of side-length $1$
nodes.genus: tilings of a hexagon of integer side-length $n$

nodes.name: Counting distinct dimer hex tilings (OEIS A066931)
nodes.statement: However, when this note was written the entry for the number of \textit{distinct} such tilings in the Online Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences (OEIS) consisted of little more than a table for $0 \le n \le 4$ and a brief discussion of those values \cite{A066931}. The aim of this note is to pull together the relevant facts and allow the entry to be improved.
nodes.statement_short: Determine A066931$(n)$, the number of hexagon tilings distinct up to the symmetries of the hexagon.

nodes.name: Symmetry group of the hexagon $D_{12}$
nodes.statement: The symmetry group of the hexagon is the dihedral group of order $12$, $D_{12}$, which has the presentation $\langle f, r \mid f^2 = r^6 = (fr)^2 = e\rangle$ where, for our geometric purposes, $f$ (for ``flip'') represents a reflection around a diameter and $r$ (for ``rotation'') represents a rotation by $60^\circ$.
nodes.statement_short: The hexagon's symmetry group is $D_{12} = \langle f, r \mid f^2 = r^6 = (fr)^2 = e\rangle$ with $f$ a reflection and $r$ a $60^\circ$ rotation.
differentia: which has the presentation $\langle f, r \mid f^2 = r^6 = (fr)^2 = e\rangle$
$f$ (for ``flip'') represents a reflection around a diameter

nodes.name: Choice of reflection axis and clash with Stanley's complementation transform
nodes.statement: At a group-theoretic level it doesn't matter whether we take the reflection to be around a diameter that passes through two vertices of the hexagon, or through the midpoints of two edges; but for the purposes of this note it is taken to pass through two vertices. Unfortunately, $fr$ then corresponds to Stanley's complementation tranform, so a rewrite may be in order to unify the two presentations.
nodes.statement_short: The reflection is fixed to pass through two vertices, which makes $fr$ (not $f$) Stanley's complementation transform.

nodes.name: Subgroup poset of $D_{12}$ as parameterised maximal chains
nodes.statement: The subgroup poset of $D_{12}$ contains $16$ subgroups, and the poset can be expressed entirely in terms of a handful of parameterised maximal chains: \begin{tabular}{ll} $\langle e\rangle < \langle r^a \rangle < \langle r \rangle < \langle f, r \rangle$ & $a \in \{2, 3\}$ \\ $\langle e\rangle < \langle r^a \rangle < \langle fr^b, r^a \rangle < \langle f, r \rangle$ & $a \in \{2, 3\}$, $b \in \{0, 1\}$ \\ $\langle e\rangle < \langle fr^a \rangle < \langle fr^{a \mod b}, r^b \rangle < \langle f, r \rangle$ & $a \in \{0, 1\}$, $b \in \{2, 3\}$ \end{tabular}
nodes.statement_short: $D_{12}$ has $16$ subgroups, and its subgroup poset is generated by three families of parameterised maximal chains.
conclusions: The subgroup poset of $D_{12}$ contains $16$ subgroups
the poset can be expressed entirely in terms of a handful of parameterised maximal chains

nodes.name: $\#c(g)$ — tilings with at least the symmetries of $g$
nodes.statement: If we denote the number of tilings which have at least the symmetries of $g \le \langle f, r\rangle$ by $\#c(g)$

nodes.name: M\"obius-inversion formula for A066931$(n)$
nodes.statement: If we denote the number of tilings which have at least the symmetries of $g \le \langle f, r\rangle$ by $\#c(g)$ then the number of tilings having exactly the symmetries of $g$ is given by the M\"obius function of the incidence algebra of this poset: $\sum_{h \le \langle f, r\rangle} \mu(g, h) \#c(h)$. We then normalise each by its index in $\langle f, r\rangle$, since we want the number of tilings corresponding to a single coset. Thus the desired value is $$\textrm{A066931}(n) = \sum_{g \le \langle f, r\rangle} \frac{1}{[D_{12} : g]} \sum_{h \le \langle f, r\rangle} \mu(g, h) \#c(h)$$
nodes.statement_short: A066931$(n)$ equals the index-weighted sum over subgroups of the M\"obius inversion of $\#c$ over the subgroup poset.
assumptions: If we denote the number of tilings which have at least the symmetries of $g \le \langle f, r\rangle$ by $\#c(g)$
conclusions: the number of tilings having exactly the symmetries of $g$ is given by the M\"obius function of the incidence algebra of this poset: $\sum_{h \le \langle f, r\rangle} \mu(g, h) \#c(h)$
$$\textrm{A066931}(n) = \sum_{g \le \langle f, r\rangle} \frac{1}{[D_{12} : g]} \sum_{h \le \langle f, r\rangle} \mu(g, h) \#c(h)$$

nodes.name: Ten conjugacy classes vs sixteen subgroups
nodes.statement: At this point, it is worth noting that although there are $16$ subgroups, there are only $10$ conjugacy groups because the $9$ subgroups which contain only reflections each have three choices of axis / axes. Thus there is no disagreement with Stanley's list of 10 symmetries of plane partitions \cite{Stanley86}.
nodes.statement_short: The $16$ subgroups collapse to $10$ conjugacy classes, matching Stanley's 10 plane-partition symmetry classes.

nodes.name: Weight-cancelled formula for A066931$(n)$
nodes.statement: Once we take that into account and work through the numbers, we find that some of the weights cancel out, leaving $$\textrm{A066931}(n) = \frac{\#c\langle e\rangle + 3\#c\langle f\rangle + 3\#c\langle fr\rangle +\#c\langle r^3\rangle + 2\#c\langle r^2\rangle + 2\#c\langle r\rangle}{12}$$
nodes.statement_short: After cancellation only six subgroup terms survive, giving A066931$(n)$ as a weighted average of $\#c\langle e\rangle, \#c\langle f\rangle, \#c\langle fr\rangle, \#c\langle r^3\rangle, \#c\langle r^2\rangle, \#c\langle r\rangle$ over $12$.
assumptions: Once we take that into account and work through the numbers
conclusions: $$\textrm{A066931}(n) = \frac{\#c\langle e\rangle + 3\#c\langle f\rangle + 3\#c\langle fr\rangle +\#c\langle r^3\rangle + 2\#c\langle r^2\rangle + 2\#c\langle r\rangle}{12}$$

nodes.name: MacMahon's box formula for $\#c\langle e\rangle$ (A008793)
nodes.statement: $\#c\langle e\rangle$ is the most studied of the cases, being simply the number of tilings (Stanley's case 1). It is A008793 in OEIS, and has formula $\#c\langle e\rangle(n) = \prod_{i=0}^{n-1} \frac{i!(i+2n)!}{(i+n)!^2}$ \cite{MacMahon16}.
nodes.statement_short: The total number of tilings is MacMahon's product $\prod_{i=0}^{n-1} i!(i+2n)!/(i+n)!^2$ (A008793).
assumptions: $\#c\langle e\rangle$ is the most studied of the cases, being simply the number of tilings (Stanley's case 1)

nodes.name: Andrews' formula for symmetric plane partitions, $\#c\langle f\rangle$ (A049505)
nodes.statement: $\#c\langle f\rangle$ is A049505, the ``number of symmetric plane partitions in n-cube'' (Stanley's case 2), with formula $\#c\langle f\rangle(n) = \prod_{i=0}^{n-1} \frac{(2i)!(i+2n)!}{(2i+n)!(i+n)!}$ (with a change of index from the OEIS entry for consistency with $\#c\langle e\rangle$) \cite{Andrews78}.
nodes.statement_short: Reflection-symmetric tilings are counted by Andrews' product $\prod_{i=0}^{n-1} (2i)!(i+2n)!/((2i+n)!(i+n)!)$ (A049505).
assumptions: $\#c\langle f\rangle$ is A049505, the ``number of symmetric plane partitions in n-cube'' (Stanley's case 2)

nodes.name: $\#c\langle fr\rangle$ vanishes for odd $n$
nodes.statement: $\#c\langle fr\rangle$ is A181119, ``transpose-complementary plane partitions'' (Stanley's case 6), but there's a slight catch. It is non-zero only for even $n$; there is a simple geometric explanation.
nodes.statement_short: Transpose-complementary tilings exist only for even $n$, for a geometric reason.
assumptions: $\#c\langle fr\rangle$ is A181119, ``transpose-complementary plane partitions'' (Stanley's case 6)
conclusions: It is non-zero only for even $n$

nodes.name: Geometric pairing argument for the $\langle fr\rangle$ parity obstruction
nodes.statement: The axis of symmetry bisects $2n$ triangles, which must pair up along the axis because otherwise they would be forced to pair with two triangles to maintain the symmetry. But the pairs start at the centre of the hexagon, so if $n$ is odd there are two triangles on opposite edges which can't be paired. (See figure 1).
nodes.statement_short: Count the $2n$ triangles bisected by the axis; they must pair along it, which is impossible for odd $n$.

nodes.name: Triangles on the axis must pair along it
nodes.statement: The axis of symmetry bisects $2n$ triangles, which must pair up along the axis because otherwise they would be forced to pair with two triangles to maintain the symmetry.
nodes.statement_short: Establish that the $2n$ axis-bisected triangles must be paired with each other along the axis.

nodes.name: Odd $n$ leaves two unpairable triangles
nodes.statement: But the pairs start at the centre of the hexagon, so if $n$ is odd there are two triangles on opposite edges which can't be paired. (See figure 1).
nodes.statement_short: Conclude the pairing fails for odd $n$, since two edge triangles are left over.

nodes.name: Figure 1 — axis-bisected triangles pairing along the axis
nodes.statement: for $\langle fr\rangle$ symmetry, the small triangles which the axis bisects must pair up along the axis.

nodes.name: Proctor's inflated formula for $\#c\langle fr\rangle(2m)$ (A181119)
nodes.statement: The upshot is that the given formula must be inflated as $\#c\langle fr\rangle(2m) = \binom{3m-1}{m} \prod_{i=0}^{2m-3} \frac{(i+4m)!(2i+2)!}{(2i+2m+2)!(i+2m)!}$ \cite{Proctor88}.
nodes.statement_short: For even $n = 2m$, transpose-complementary tilings number $\binom{3m-1}{m}\prod_{i=0}^{2m-3}(i+4m)!(2i+2)!/((2i+2m+2)!(i+2m)!)$.
assumptions: The upshot is that the given formula must be inflated

nodes.name: $\#c\langle r^3\rangle$ missing from OEIS
nodes.statement: $\#c\langle r^3\rangle$ is, astonishingly, not in OEIS!\footnote{Update: it is now A259049.}
nodes.statement_short: The self-complementary count was absent from OEIS at the time of writing; it is now A259049.

nodes.name: $\#c\langle r^3\rangle$ vanishes for odd $n$
nodes.statement: It corresponds to Stanley's case 5 (self-complementary plane partitions), and is non-zero only for even $n$, for a slightly different reason.
nodes.statement_short: Self-complementary tilings (Stanley's case 5) exist only for even $n$.
assumptions: It corresponds to Stanley's case 5 (self-complementary plane partitions)

nodes.name: Half-hexagon surplus argument for the $\langle r^3\rangle$ parity obstruction
nodes.statement: If we divide the hexagon into six large triangles by drawing the diameters through its vertices, each of these large triangles has $\frac{n(n+1)}{2}$ small triangles in one orientation and $\frac{(n-1)n}{2}$ small triangles in another orientation. For $\langle r^3\rangle$ we can consider a half-hexagon formed from three of the large triangles: the symmetry will give us the tiling of the other half. This half-hexagon has a surplus of $n$ triangles in one orientation; therefore there must be $n$ triangles along the diameter which pair across into the other half-hexagon. (See figure 2). By the rotational symmetry, these $n$ triangles must be paired up, but if $n$ is odd this is impossible.
nodes.statement_short: Count orientations in a half-hexagon: its surplus of $n$ triangles must pair across the diameter, impossible when $n$ is odd.

nodes.name: Count small triangles per large triangle
nodes.statement: If we divide the hexagon into six large triangles by drawing the diameters through its vertices, each of these large triangles has $\frac{n(n+1)}{2}$ small triangles in one orientation and $\frac{(n-1)n}{2}$ small triangles in another orientation.
nodes.statement_short: Set up the six-large-triangle decomposition and count small triangles by orientation.

nodes.name: Reduce to a half-hexagon
nodes.statement: For $\langle r^3\rangle$ we can consider a half-hexagon formed from three of the large triangles: the symmetry will give us the tiling of the other half.
nodes.statement_short: Use the $\langle r^3\rangle$ symmetry to reduce the problem to one half-hexagon.

nodes.name: Surplus of $n$ triangles must cross the diameter
nodes.statement: This half-hexagon has a surplus of $n$ triangles in one orientation; therefore there must be $n$ triangles along the diameter which pair across into the other half-hexagon. (See figure 2).
nodes.statement_short: Derive that exactly $n$ triangles must pair across the diameter.

nodes.name: Odd $n$ makes the crossing pairing impossible
nodes.statement: By the rotational symmetry, these $n$ triangles must be paired up, but if $n$ is odd this is impossible.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude the count vanishes for odd $n$.

nodes.name: Figure 2 — $n$ small triangles paired across the diameter
nodes.statement: for $\langle r^3\rangle$ symmetry, exactly $n$ small triangles must be in pairs which cross the diameter.

nodes.name: Stanley's formula for self-complementary tilings $\#c\langle r^3\rangle(2m)$
nodes.statement: For even $n$ we have $\#c\langle r^3\rangle(2m) = \#c\langle e\rangle(m)^2$ \cite{Stanley86}.

nodes.name: Andrews' formula for cyclically symmetric plane partitions, $\#c\langle r^2\rangle$ (A006366)
nodes.statement: $\#c\langle r^2\rangle$ is A006366, ``number of cyclically symmetric plane partitions in the n-cube'' (Stanley's case 3), with formula $\#c\langle r^2\rangle(n) = \prod_{i=0}^{n-1} \frac{(3i+2)(3i)!(i+2n)!}{(2i+n)!(2i+n+1)!}$ \cite{Andrews79}.
nodes.statement_short: Cyclically symmetric tilings are counted by Andrews' product $\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}(3i+2)(3i)!(i+2n)!/((2i+n)!(2i+n+1)!)$ (A006366).
assumptions: $\#c\langle r^2\rangle$ is A006366, ``number of cyclically symmetric plane partitions in the n-cube'' (Stanley's case 3)

nodes.name: Kuperberg's formula for $\#c\langle r\rangle(2m)$ (A049503)
nodes.statement: $\#c\langle r\rangle$ is A049503, which is cryptically described as ``A005130$^2$'' and ``Expansion of generating function $A_{QT}^{(1)}(4n)$''. It corresponds to the cyclically symmetric and self-complementary plane partitions (Stanley's case 9). Note that again we must inflate the sequence (since $\langle r^3\rangle \le \langle r\rangle$ the same argument applies), and when we do so we get that $\#c\langle r\rangle(2m) = \prod_{i=0}^{m-1} \frac{(3i+1)!^2}{(i+m)!^2}$ \cite{Kuperberg94}.
nodes.statement_short: Cyclically symmetric self-complementary tilings, after the same even-$n$ inflation, number $\prod_{i=0}^{m-1}(3i+1)!^2/(i+m)!^2$.
assumptions: It corresponds to the cyclically symmetric and self-complementary plane partitions (Stanley's case 9)
again we must inflate the sequence (since $\langle r^3\rangle \le \langle r\rangle$ the same argument applies)
nodes.origin_citation: Kuperberg 1994, Symmetries of plane partitions and the permanent-determinant method

nodes.name: Explicit baseline and inflated correction for A066931$(n)$
nodes.statement_short: A066931$(n)$ is a three-term product-formula baseline plus, for even $n = 2m$, a three-term correction from the $\langle fr\rangle, \langle r^3\rangle, \langle r\rangle$ cases.
